scenario: AITA for asking for more per-diem? | I'm a woman working in a career that's about 98% male. I am the first woman my company has ever hired. The company offers per-diem pay when you're sent to work more than an hour away. The amount is not a lot, but it's enough for a shared hotel room and a bit left over for food. A few guys choose keep the money and sleep in their cars, or take a long commute home every night if it's 2 hours or less. I was asked to go on a job 4hrs away, 12 hour shifts, so commuting each day is not an option. I'm not comfortable sharing a room with men I don't know well, or sleeping in my car. I called the project manager and said I'd go if he increased the per-diem enough to pay for a single room. He said yes. My male coworkers are now mad that I 'asked for special treatment' and shared rooms are 'just how things are done in this industry'. I feel that if they wanted their own rooms, no one has ever stopped them from asking. AITA?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Let me know if you’d like help with specific messages or designs!

The Company’s Per-Diem Policy Was Never "Neutral"** - The per-diem was **designed for men’s needs**, not women’s. A shared room covers a man’s expenses, but a **single room is a reasonable accommodation** when safety is a concern. - **You’re not the first woman to face this.** Many industries (aviation, oil rigs, fieldwork) have had to **negotiate for single rooms** because the default assumption was always male. Your company’s policy was **implicitly discriminatory**—not because you asked, but because it didn’t account for women’s realities. - **HR should have addressed this years ago.** If this is the first woman hired, the company likely **never considered** how policies affect women. Your request forced them to **confront an oversight**. --- ### **3. The Backlash Is About Power, Not Logic** - Men in your position **didn’t ask for single rooms** because they **never had to**. They assumed the policy was fair because it worked for them. That’s **not "how things are done"**—that’s **male privilege in action**. - Their anger isn’t about **fairness**; it’s about **losing a "perk"** they took for granted. They’re upset that **someone called out an unfair system**, not that you asked for a reasonable adjustment. - **This is a classic "bro culture" reaction.** In male-dominated fields, women who push back for safety or fairness are often **gaslit into thinking they’re "too sensitive"**—but you’re not. You’re **holding the company accountable**. --- ### **4. What You Did Was the Right Thing (And Here’s How to Handle the Pushback)** #### **A. You Were Entitled to a Single Room** - **Safety > comfort.** If a man in your position had a medical condition (e.g., sleep apnea, back problems) requiring a private room, would anyone question it? **No.** But because it’s a **gendered issue**, suddenly it’s "special treatment." - **You didn’t ask for more than what’s fair.** The per-diem was **never designed for women’s needs**, so adjusting it to cover a single room is **not "extra"**—it’s **correcting an imbalance**. #### **B. How to Respond to the Backlash** 1. **Stay calm and factual.** - *"I’m not asking for special treatment—I’m asking for the same level of safety that’s expected for anyone in this role. If a man had a medical reason for a single room, would anyone question it?"* - *"The per-diem policy was never designed with women’s safety in mind. Adjusting it to cover a single room isn’t about me—it’s about making the policy fair for everyone."* 2. **Document everything.** - If they continue to resist, **email HR** with: - *"I’d like to discuss accommodations for safety during out-of-town assignments, as the current per-diem does not cover a single room. Can we schedule a time to review this?"* - **Save all communications** in case this becomes a larger issue. 3. **Find allies.** - Are there **other women in the company** (even in other departments)? If not, **connect with women in similar industries** (LinkedIn, professional groups) to share experiences. - If you’re the **only woman**, your request **automatically puts you in a vulnerable position**. Lean on **HR or a mentor** to help mediate. 4. **Escalate if needed.** - If the company **refuses to budge**, this could be a **discrimination issue**. Consult: - **Your company’s HR policies** (do they have a harassment/safety protocol?). - **External resources** (e.g., [EEOC](https://www.eeoc.gov/) in the U.S., or local gender equality organizations). - **Legal advice** if the backlash turns hostile. --- ### **5. The Broader Problem: Why This Happens** This isn’t just about **one company**—it’s a **systemic issue** in male-dominated fields: - **"Bro culture" normalizes unsafe conditions** for men but **punishes women for asking for basic safety**. - **Per-diem policies are rarely audited for gender bias.** They assume a **default "man"** who can handle rough conditions. - **Women are often the "last to be hired" in these fields**, so companies **haven’t had to think about accommodations** until now. **Your action is part of a larger movement** to **challenge these norms**. You’re not being unreasonable—you’re **holding the company to a standard they never enforced for themselves**. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Did Nothing Wrong** ✅ **You prioritized safety** (which is non-negotiable). ✅ **You called out an unfair policy** (which needed to be fixed). ✅ **You didn’t ask for anything unreasonable**—just **what should have been standard all along**. The real issue isn’t **you**—it’s that **this company (and many like it) operates on outdated, male-centric assumptions**. The fact that men are upset isn’t about **fairness**; it’s about **losing a privilege they never questioned**. **Keep pushing back.** If they can’t adjust, **find a company that will**. Your career—and your safety—are worth it. --- ### **Bonus: What to Say to Your Coworkers (If You Want to)** If you’re open to it, you could try: *"I get that this is new for everyone, but safety isn’t a luxury—it’s a basic expectation. If a man had a medical reason for a private room, no one would bat an eye. I’m just asking for the same standard. Let’s make sure the policy works for everyone, not just the default assumption."* (If they still resist, **don’t engage further**—let HR handle it.) --- **You’re doing the right thing.** Keep going. 💪
